title: C++ Classes and OOP: Quick Revision
summary: Night-before revision of C++ classes: constructors, destructors, the rule of three/five/zero, inheritance, virtual dispatch, abstract classes and operator overloading.

chapters.title: Classes, Structs and Construction
points: class vs struct: the only difference is default access (class = private, struct = public), also default inheritance (private vs public)
Constructor has no return type and runs once per object; the compiler generates a default constructor only if you declare no constructor at all
Member initializer list (Foo(int a): x(a), y(a*2) {}) initializes members before the body runs; required for const members, reference members and members without a default constructor
Members are initialized in declaration order, not initializer-list order, so reordering the list does not change it (and can trigger -Wreorder bugs when one member uses another)
Mark single-argument constructors explicit to block implicit conversions like Foo f = 5; delegating constructors (Foo(): Foo(0) {}) reuse one constructor

chapters.title: Destructors and the Rule of Three, Five and Zero
points: Destructor ~Foo() runs when an object leaves scope or is deleted; members are destroyed in reverse declaration order, then bases
Rule of three: if you need a custom destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, you almost certainly need all three (shallow copy of a raw pointer causes double delete)
Rule of five adds move constructor and move assignment (Foo(Foo&&) noexcept); mark them noexcept so std::vector moves instead of copies on growth
Rule of zero: hold resources in std::unique_ptr, std::vector, std::string so you write none of the five and the compiler-generated ones are correct

Copy assignment must handle self-assignment (a = a) safely; copy-and-swap idiom (operator=(Foo other) { swap(*this, other); }) gives this plus exception safety; =default and =delete explicitly keep or remove special members

chapters.title: Inheritance and Virtual Functions
points: Public inheritance models is-a; derived constructor calls the base constructor first (Derived(): Base(args) {}), destruction runs in reverse order
Without virtual, calls bind at compile time by the pointer's static type; with virtual they bind at run time by the object's dynamic type
vtable: one table of function pointers per class with virtuals; each object carries a hidden vptr to it, costing one pointer per object and one indirect call per virtual call
Use override on every overriding function so signature mismatches become compile errors; final blocks further overriding or inheriting

Object slicing: passing or assigning a Derived by value to a Base copies only the Base part and loses polymorphism, so use references or pointers; never call virtual functions in a constructor or destructor (they resolve to the current class, not the most derived)

chapters.title: Abstract Classes and Virtual Destructors
points: Pure virtual function (virtual void draw() const = 0;) makes a class abstract: it cannot be instantiated, only used as an interface via pointers or references
A derived class stays abstract until it overrides every pure virtual function
A pure virtual function may still have a body, and a pure virtual destructor must have a definition (virtual ~Base() = 0; Base::~Base() {})
Base class with virtual functions needs a virtual destructor: deleting a Derived through a Base* with a non-virtual destructor is undefined behavior and skips ~Derived
Interface example: struct Shape { virtual ~Shape() = default; virtual double area() const = 0; }; held as std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape>> for runtime polymorphism

chapters.title: Operator Overloading
points: Overloaded operator is a function named operator+ etc.; you cannot add new operators or change precedence, and :: . .* ?: sizeof cannot be overloaded
Member vs free function: = [] () -> must be members; symmetric binary operators (a + b, a == b, operator<<) are best free functions so implicit conversion works on the left operand
Implement += as a member, then build + on top of it (Foo operator+(Foo a, const Foo& b) { return a += b; }); return *this by reference from assignment-style operators
Stream output: std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Foo& f) { return os << f.x; } is a free function (often friend) returning the stream for chaining

C++20 spaceship: auto operator<=>(const Foo&) const = default; generates all six comparisons; prefix ++ returns Foo&, postfix ++(int) returns the old value by copy and is slower; mark const methods const so they work on const objects

chapters.title: C++ OOP Cheat Sheet
points: Special members: default ctor, copy ctor, copy assign, move ctor, move assign, destructor; prefer rule of zero, else define all five
Init order: bases, then members in declaration order, then ctor body; destroy in exact reverse
Checklist for a polymorphic base: virtual ~Base(), override on every override, no slicing (pass by reference or pointer), no virtual calls in ctor/dtor
explicit on one-argument ctors, noexcept on moves, const on methods that do not modify state
Operator rules: = [] () -> are members; << and symmetric binary operators are free; += first then +; <=> = default in C++20
